accepted.question_text: Give a mathematically meaningful characterization of what should count as an interesting or natural mathematical question.

evidence.quote: 2. What is an interesting or natural mathematical question? (G. J. Chaitin)

accepted.question_text: Determine how frequently an interesting or natural mathematical question is independent of the usual axioms.

evidence.quote: 3. How often is such a question independent of the usual axioms? (I suspect the answer is "Quite often!") (G. J. Chaitin)

accepted.question_text: Show that some classical open problem in number theory, for example the Riemann hypothesis, is independent of the usual axioms.

evidence.quote: 4. Show that a classical open question in number theory, such as the Riemann hypothesis, is independent of the usual axioms. (I suspect that this is often the case, but that it cannot be proven.) (G. J. Chaitin)

accepted.question_text: The non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are described in the source as uniformly distributed modulo 1 after the displayed normalization. Do those non-trivial zeros form a random sequence?

evidence.quote: 5. The non-trivial zeros of Riemann's Zeta function are uniformly distributed ... is uniformly distributed modulo 1. Do non-trivial zeros of Riemann's Zeta function form a random sequence? (C. Calude)

accepted.question_text: In mathematical practice, should incompleteness be treated as a central phenomenon rather than dismissed as a red herring?

evidence.quote: 6. When doing mathematics, should we take incompleteness seriously or is it a red herring? (I believe that we should take incompleteness very seriously indeed.) (G. J. Chaitin)

accepted.question_text: Is mathematics quasi-empirical, in the sense that mathematical research ought to be conducted more like physics?

evidence.quote: 7. Is mathematics quasi-empirical? In other words, should mathematics be done more like physics is done? (I believe the answer to both questions is "Yes.") (G. J. Chaitin)

accepted.question_text: Further develop the theory of program-size complexity for infinite computations, and in particular clarify its relation to algorithmic probability.

evidence.quote: 8. Further develop the theory of program-size complexity for infinite computations. Particularly, study the relations between program-size complexity and algorithmic probability. (G. J. Chaitin)

accepted.question_text: Extend Chaitin complexity from finite strings to infinite strings, either by using non-terminating programs that generate infinite strings over infinite time or by using computational models that process infinite strings in finite time, such as cellular automata or functions on the reals.

evidence.quote: 9. Chaitin complexity has been defined for finite strings. It would be interesting to extend it to infinite strings. Two ways can be envisaged: (a) using non-terminating programs ... generating infinite strings in an infinite amount of time; (b) using computational models dealing with infinite strings in finite amounts of time (cellular automata, functions on reals, etc.). (F. Geurts)

accepted.question_text: Determine whether deterministic chaos in discrete-time dynamical systems can be described in terms of Chaitin complexity, and clarify how Chaitin complexity relates to the usual definition of chaos via sensitivity to initial conditions, topological transitivity, and density of periodic points.

evidence.quote: 10. Is it possible to describe the "deterministic chaos" by means of Chaitin complexity? Discrete-time dynamical systems are called "chaotic" if they are sensitive to initial conditions. What is the relation between this definition (using topological transitivity and density of periodic points) and Chaitin complexity? (F. Geurts)

accepted.question_text: Study the transformations that preserve random strings and random sequences.

evidence.quote: 11. Study the transformations that preserve random strings and sequences. (C. Calude, H. Jürgensen)

accepted.question_text: Further develop algorithmic information theory for bi-infinite sequences and, more generally, for constructive cpo's, possibly using bi-infinite cellular automata as computational models.

evidence.quote: 12. Further develop algorithmic information theory for bi-infinite sequences and, more generally, for constructive cpo's. (C. Calude, H. Jürgensen) An idea would be to use bi-infinite cellular automata as computational models. (F. Geurts)

accepted.question_text: Identify natural properties of randomness that are satisfied by Chaitin-random strings but not by Kolmogorov-random strings, given that every Chaitin-random string is Kolmogorov random but not conversely.

evidence.quote: 13. Every Chaitin random string is Kolmogorov random, but the converse is not true. Identify natural properties associated to "randomness" which are satisfied by Chaitin random strings, but not by Kolmogorov random strings. (C. Calude)
15. Axiomatize algorithmic information theory. (H. Jürgensen)

accepted.question_text: Study constructions and objects in constructive mathematics from the viewpoint of program-size complexity, where constructive mathematics is taken to mean mathematics together with the principle that existence coincides with computability.

evidence.quote: 16. Constructive mathematics is essentially mathematics plus the assumption that "existence = computability". Constructions and objects in constructive mathematics have been studied from the point of view of dynamic complexities and it would be interesting to study them also from the point of view of program-size complexity. (C. Calude)

accepted.question_text: Derive incompleteness results for determining quantum algorithmic information.

evidence.quote: 17. Derive incompleteness results for the determination of quantum algorithmic information. (K. Svozil)

accepted.question_text: Determine whether there exists a model of computation in which the Invariance Theorem remains valid for time complexity as well.

evidence.quote: 18. Is there any model of computation in which the Invariance Theorem holds true also for the time complexity? (C. Calude)

accepted.question_text: Define and study symmetry for random strings and random sequences, and determine whether lack of symmetry should be regarded as evidence of non-randomness.

evidence.quote: 19. Define and study the symmetry of random strings and sequences. Is the absence of symmetry a symptom of non-randomness? (C. Calude)

accepted.question_text: Study binary operations that preserve random strings or random sequences.

evidence.quote: 20. Study binary operations which preserve random strings/sequences. (T. Odor)

accepted.question_text: Let the degree of randomness of a finite string x be measured by comparing the complexity of x with the complexities of all strings of the same length. Extend this notion to randomness with respect to an arbitrary finite set M, in a way that respects the intuition that if M has m elements and admits a description whose length is negligible compared with log m, then almost all elements of M should have near-maximal complexity, close to log m, relative to M.
accepted.context_brief: Randomness relative to a finite set

evidence.quote: 22. The degree of randomness of a string x depends upon the complexity of the string x compared with the complexities of all strings having the same length. Extend this definition of randomness "with respect to an arbitrary finite set". An appropriate solution should conform the following intuitive fact: if a finite set of strings M containing m elements, where m is very large, can be defined by a program of length negligible when compared with log m, then almost all elements of M should have maximal complexity (which is close to log m); these strings should be "random" with respect to M. (C. Calude)
